title: Measurements
text:
Stomata are microscopic pores on leaf surfaces, each flanked by a pair of guard cells. Their geometry is a key indicator of plant physiology: stomatal size and aperture regulate gas exchange (CO₂/O₂) and water loss (transpiration). Accurate morphometric measurements allow researchers to:

Compare stomatal morphology across genotypes, species, or treatments
Quantify stress responses (drought, heat) through pore aperture changes
Estimate stomatal conductance from geometric proxies

The figure below shows a single stoma from a real brightfield microscopy image (training dataset), with the YOLO segmentation polygons and all four measurement lines overlaid. The green outline is the stoma body mask (class 1); the cyan outline is the pore/aperture mask (class 0):

title: Measurements
text:
Trait Definitions
PSCA reports every measurement in both pixels and micrometres (µm). Pixel-to-micrometre conversion uses the calibration constant:
\[
\text{PX\_TO\_UM} = \frac{50.0\,\mu\text{m}}{451.3958\,\text{px}} \approx 0.1108\,\mu\text{m/px}
\]






Note



This calibration is specific to the microscope/objective used by the Pollination Ecology Group. If you change optics, update PX_TO_UM in src/extract_traits.py.




1. Major Axis Length (major_axis_len_um)


📏 Major Axis — Full Stoma Length


The longest dimension of the minimum-area bounding rectangle fitted around the stoma mask. This corresponds to the longitudinal axis of the stoma, typically oriented parallel to the epidermal cell rows.


stoma_major_length_px = max(rect_width, rect_height) → × PX_TO_UM


How it is computed: cv2.minAreaRect() fits the tightest possible rotated rectangle around the stoma polygon. The longer of the two rectangle sides is taken as the major axis.
Biological meaning: Reflects overall stoma size. Larger stomata are associated with polyploidy, shade adaptation, and certain stress responses.



2. Minor Axis Length (minor_axis_len_um)


📏 Minor Axis — Full Stoma Width


The length of the minor axis line (perpendicular to the major axis) where it intersects the full stoma outline. Measured by projecting the minor-axis direction through the stoma polygon.


stoma_minor_length_px = minor_axis_line ∩ stoma_polygon → length → × PX_TO_UM


How it is computed:

The minor axis direction is extracted from the bounding rectangle angle.
An infinitely long line is cast through the stoma centroid along that direction.
The intersection of this line with the stoma polygon gives the chord length = minor axis.

Biological meaning: Width of the closed stoma. Together with the major axis, this gives a shape index (eccentricity / aspect ratio).



3. Pore Minor Length (pore_minor_len_um)


🔵 Pore Width — Aperture Diameter


The width of the central pore (aperture) measured along the same minor axis direction as above. PSCA detects the pore as a separate segmentation class and intersects it with the same minor axis line.


center_minor_length_px = minor_axis_line ∩ pore_polygon → length → × PX_TO_UM


How it is computed: The model segments the pore as class 0 (center) and the full stoma as class 1. The pore polygon is intersected with the same minor axis line used for the stoma.
Biological meaning: The most ecophysiologically important trait — directly proportional to stomatal conductance (g_s). A wider pore = higher gas exchange and transpiration.



4. Guard Cell Width (guard_cell_width_um)


🟢 Guard Cell Width — Thickness of One Guard Cell


Estimated as half the difference between the stoma width and the pore width along the minor axis. Represents the radial thickness of a single guard cell.


guard_cell_width_px = (stoma_minor_length_px − pore_minor_length_px) / 2 → × PX_TO_UM


How it is computed: Since the minor axis passes through both guard cells symmetrically, the stoma width = pore width + 2 × guard cell width.
Biological meaning: Guard cell thickness correlates with turgor potential and mechanical properties of the cell wall. Thicker guard cells tend to open with less turgor.

title: Measurements
Inference Pipeline
text:
PSCA is a containerised batch pipeline that:

Downloads images from CESNET S3 storage
Runs YOLOv11 instance segmentation on each image
Extracts geometric traits from the segmentation masks
Saves results to a CSV and uploads it back to S3

The pipeline runs as a Kubernetes Job — no local GPU required.

Architecture

title: Inference Pipeline
text:
Step-by-Step

Step 1 — Model Download
If the model is not already cached at MODEL_PATH (/tmp/best.pt by default), it is downloaded from S3 at startup:
if S3_MODEL_KEY and not os.path.exists(MODEL_PATH):
    s3.download_file(S3_BUCKET, S3_MODEL_KEY, MODEL_PATH)
The model key is configured via the S3_MODEL_KEY environment variable.



Step 2 — Image Discovery
The S3 bucket is paginated to find all .jpg / .jpeg / .png files under the configured prefix:
paginator = s3.get_paginator('list_objects_v2')
pages = paginator.paginate(Bucket=S3_BUCKET, Prefix=TILE_PREFIX)
Default prefix: Ostatni/Stomata/extracted/



Step 3 — Parallel Download + Inference
Images are processed in batches of 100 to limit memory usage. Within each batch, images are downloaded concurrently using a 16-worker thread pool:
with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=FETCH_WORKERS) as executor:
    futures = [executor.submit(download_image, s3, key) for key in batch_keys]
    for future in concurrent.futures.as_completed(futures):
        key, img = future.result()
        if img is not None:
            res = process_image(model, img, image_name)






Note



YOLO inference itself runs sequentially on the GPU. Only image downloading is parallelised — this hides S3 network latency behind GPU compute time.





Step 4 — Trait Extraction
For each image, process_image() in extract_traits.py:

Runs YOLO inference → gets segmentation masks + class labels
Separates masks into stoma (class 1) and pore (class 0) lists
For each stoma, finds the matching pore (containment check → nearest-neighbour fallback)
Computes the minor axis via cv2.minAreaRect() and shapely intersection
Returns a list of measurement dicts

See the Measurements page for full trait definitions.



Step 5 — Output & Upload
Results are collected into a pandas DataFrame, saved to a local CSV, then uploaded to S3:
S3_OUTPUT_KEY = "Ostatni/Stomata/stomata_traits.csv"
Intermediate saves happen every 1000 images to guard against job interruption.

title: Plant Stomata Counter-Analyser
text:
What is PSCA?
The Plant Stomata Counter-Analyser (PSCA) is an end-to-end automated pipeline developed by the Pollination Ecology Group to replace manual stomata counting in microscopy images. It combines a fine-tuned YOLOv11 instance segmentation model with geometric post-processing to extract biologically meaningful traits at scale.






TipQuick Start



Jump to the Measurements page to understand what gets measured and why, or visit the Pipeline page to see how the system works end-to-end.

title: Plant Stomata Counter-Analyser
text:
Key Features







Feature
Description




🔬 Instance segmentation
Detects each individual stoma and its pore separately


📐 Geometric trait extraction
4 morphometric measurements per stoma in both pixels and µm


☁️ Cloud-native
Reads images from and writes results to CESNET S3


⚡ High-throughput
Parallel image download with multi-worker thread pool


🐳 Containerised
Runs as a Kubernetes Job — no local GPU required


📊 CSV output
One row per stoma, ready for R/Python downstream analysis

title: Plant Stomata Counter-Analyser
text:
Measured Traits at a Glance
Each detected stoma produces four geometric measurements:
major_axis_len_um   — Full length of the stoma (µm)
minor_axis_len_um   — Full width of the stoma (µm)
pore_minor_len_um   — Width of the central pore opening (µm)
guard_cell_width_um — Thickness of a single guard cell (µm)
See the Measurements page for a fully annotated diagram and trait definitions.

title: Cloud Storage Setup
text:
ImportantCredentials



Ask the Project Lead for the team access_key_id and secret_access_key before starting. Do not share them via Slack or email — use a secure channel.
Goal: Mount the team’s CESNET S3 bucket as a local folder so you can drag-and-drop microscopy images and retrieve results without a browser.

title: Cloud Storage Setup
text:
Step 0 — Install Prerequisites
You need Rclone (the connector) and a FUSE driver (so Rclone can present the bucket as a folder).

🐧 Linux🪟 Windows🍎 macOS


sudo apt install rclone fuse3



Download Rclone for Windows, unzip, place rclone.exe in e.g. C:\rclone\, add to PATH.
Download and install WinFsp — required for mounting.



brew install rclone
Then download and install macFUSE.

Note (Apple Silicon): You may need to allow kernel extensions in Recovery Mode for macFUSE. Check if fuse-t works as an alternative on M1/M2/M3.

text:
Step 2 — Mount the Drive

🐧 Linux🪟 Windows🍎 macOS


One-time:
mkdir ~/cesnet_cloud
rclone mount cesnet_s3: ~/cesnet_cloud --vfs-cache-mode writes --daemon
Auto-start on login — open Startup Applications, click Add, and use this command:
rclone mount cesnet_s3: /home/YOUR_USER/cesnet_cloud --vfs-cache-mode writes --daemon


One-time (PowerShell):
mkdir C:\cesnet_cloud
rclone mount cesnet_s3: C:\cesnet_cloud --vfs-cache-mode writes

Keep this terminal open — closing it disconnects the drive.

Auto-start: Create mount_cesnet.bat with:
@echo off
start /b rclone mount cesnet_s3: Z: --vfs-cache-mode writes --no-console
Place the .bat file in shell:startup (Win + R → type shell:startup).


One-time:
mkdir ~/cesnet_cloud
rclone mount cesnet_s3: ~/cesnet_cloud --vfs-cache-mode writes --daemon
Auto-start: Create mount_cesnet.sh:
#!/bin/bash
rclone mount cesnet_s3: /Users/YOUR_USER/cesnet_cloud --vfs-cache-mode writes --daemon
Make it executable (chmod +x mount_cesnet.sh) and add it in System Settings → General → Login Items.

title: Cloud Storage Setup
text:
⚠️ Best Practices






Warning



Don’t edit large files in place. Copy the file to your local desktop first, edit it there, then copy it back. Opening a multi-GB image directly from the cloud drive will be slow.








Tip



Wait for uploads. When you drag a file into cesnet_cloud/, give it a few seconds to finish uploading before shutting down your computer.


If the drive freezes (e.g. internet loss), unmount it:



Platform
Command




Linux
fusermount -u ~/cesnet_cloud


Windows
Ctrl+C in the terminal


macOS
umount ~/cesnet_cloud
